utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Wednesday we're going to continue the proceedings, and if the registrar has no IC numbers to give us, I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Praljak straight away, and he has exactly 23 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Prosecution. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon, General. I have seven and a half more minutes from Counsel Alaburic, but I hope that I'll be able to get through my cross-examination before that. I'd like to have document P 04235 shown, please, P 04235. It's a document dated the 16th of August, 1993, and when the witness arrived and at a meeting in Zagreb, I'm sure, too, he was or had to have been informed of the previous situation. I'm going to show him what all this looked like on the ground and what the actual state of affairs was. This document is one which I as the HVO commander requested from my commanders. I asked them to provide me with a report about the situation on the battlefield and what the units there were, and then I wrote myself a report, because I was in the Uskoplje area at the time. But can you see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that at the Rama-Uskoplje battlefield 20 units were engaged with a total of 4.424 men in 20 units, and the 21st was the artillery. Do you see those facts and figures?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now look at my explanations. Out of the total number, and I'm writing this for myself, for my own purposes for the Main Staff, deduct 10 per cent for various reasons, sickness, death, and so on, and if you deduct from that all the logistics and the accompanying service and the fatigue of the men from Jajce and 40 per cent of these Sebesici people were psychologically, mentally disturbed, and part of the Bugojno people had escaped of the 5th Guards Brigade, there are only 130, the only proper unit numbering 20 men at the time, it says up at the top there, was Filipovic's, and pursuant to an oral order they are supposed to leave the area and in fact most of them have already left, and there are no Klica's men. Now, my comment is not commensurate to the thinking of the American army or foreign legion, but I see -- I see at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the accused repeat the word he said, please. Could he repeat the word. Could Mr. Praljak repeat the word he said. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we have the document raised up, please, so we can see the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end my comment is of a report that I'm writing actually to myself, I say "Fuck it." So do you see that down there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your information, when you arrived later on was -- the situation in these volunteer units was -- the situation in these volunteer units of the HVO were such that the only possible comment was precisely the comment that I wrote down on that document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, retired General, now, we were informed of this same situation by General Tole, the facts and figures are more or less the same and the same thing was confirmed at the beginning of the operation in the Uskoplje area. There were a lot of units, while very few operationally capable people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did the operation in Uskoplje fall through?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was stopped sometime in mid -- or, rather, at the end of November because we didn't have enough manpower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we're discussing this point and you were down there, I had to go back to Uskoplje in order to see to the situation there to prevent the breakthrough of the BH army into Rama.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I was involved on other assignments and tasks. I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to P 06482. 6482. The document that's going to appear is dated the 6th of November, that is to say two days before your arrival in 1993. I am issuing an order for meeting to be held and that -- to attend the meeting are all commanders of the areas, brigades, all the commanders. Bruno Busic, Ludvig Pavlovic, and other units. Do you see that order?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says in point 4 there that the meeting will take place in Tomislavgrad on the 7th of November, 1993, and that it will commence at 1800 hours. The signature there - may we have the next page, please - is Major General Slobodan Praljak. Do you see that signature? Can we have the page turned, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got it up on the screen yet. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we note -- do you agree with me there that two days before your arrival I called for a meeting of all my commanders in Tomislavgrad? And now I'd like to have the next document, 3D 00793. 3D 00793. It's the minutes from that meeting, and it says at the top that it is Tomislavgrad on the 7th of November, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and so on and so forth, and that the meeting was held on the 7th, and you can see what else it says. While we've got the first page up on our screens. This has been sent to the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Sabor parliament of the HR HB, to the government of the HR HB, and to the Main Staff of the HR HB. Can you see all that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we have the points listed with the requests, instructions, demands. The government of the HR HB should immediately sit down to hold a meeting and keep meeting until the teams visit the field and units and -- as well as to bring decisions which are commensurate to the field situation. Second, that government commissioners must be appointed with all authorisation instead of municipal HVO commissioners. Now, in your work, was it one of the most difficult things to see how the municipal organs and authorities were -- for instance, their relationship to the army and everything else?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what most of the commanders said, and those are the kinds of reports that I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't got time to elaborate the influence that existed, so we'll leave that to a later date. It talks about the mobilisation of all available manpower, and then in point 5 it says to establish rigorous control on the border with RH, referring to the fluctuation of men and goods, merchandise. Now, an individual or a group of people in Herceg-Bosna, soldiers, could they just take off their uniforms, leave their rifles, cross the border, and go to Croatia without anybody doing anything?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Check-points had been erected. Now, how far they were efficacious before my arrival, I can't say. I don't know. But with my arrival we became more rigorous in allowing people to leave Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know that today the borders between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina have more than 300 secret passages?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak of those passages. I was speaking about the check-points where control was enforced, but I'm sure there were many other points that weren't controlled and where you could cross clandestinely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we conclude that they could leave without any sanctions taken? You couldn't do anything effective to punish transgressions of that kind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in point 6 it says to stop one, and only one, command line, line of command. Now, did you encounter that problem that different people through different channels had different ways of influencing the system of command within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we tried to establish a firm line of command or chain of command. We did a lot in at that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look at the commanders, officers of the HR HB of the military districts of Tomislavgrad and Mostar. The others, for well known reasons, from Central Bosnia and Posavina were not able to arrive. May we look at page 2, please. Page 2 on the screen, please. There you have the list of names. Tell me, please, are those all the commanders from this area? Did all the commanders sign this?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see their names on the screen, and I can say that I know a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, next document is 3D 00796. 3D 00796. The document that's going to come up on your screen now refers to a meeting of a smaller number of my commanders -- or, rather, of commanders. The meeting was held in Tomislavgrad on the 26th of October, 1993. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it goes into more details and addresses the problems in a clearer fashion as regards the army. And if you take a look at the second paragraph, you will see what we're requesting. First of all, military activities are addressed, which would ensure the legitimate historical and democratic goals of the Croatian people and its survival in these areas. So we're not speaking about a state, about separation, or anything else. We're talking about democratic, legitimate goals of a constituent peoples people and its survival there. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 1 it says: "The time has come when will we're no longer able to establish the army on the basis of voluntariness, on voluntary principles. If the conditions for introducing the regular army still do not exist, we must establish mobile stand-by brigades proportionately to all the municipal territories." Do we agree that these mobile brigades mean that they're not closely connected to the territory of a municipality which with the influence that a community can wield, especially as the municipality has paid them? Is that right? Is that how we can understand this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at point 3. The same thing is repeated. "It is also necessary to adopt regulations on blocking all border crossings in order to regulate the entrance and exit of military conscripts ..." This is a problem that you encountered, too, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 4 it says: "To deal with the status of deserters." I'm sure you had the problem of deserters and had to deal with the question.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have that problem, and 3.500 or 4.000 people were convicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there a lot of people who were put in prison?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a single person was -- who was convicted for desertion actually served a prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have information like that when I was down there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 5 it says to: "Regulate the composition of the active military police and instructions as well as criteria for work contain special instructions on arrest and bringing into custody deserters." So here we're dealing with deserters again. Are you aware that the people that remain on the battlefront find it very difficult to see other people fleeing and nothing done to punish them? Does that undermine the morale of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it does in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the HVO had a set of rules on discipline?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We," in point 7, "demand that a disciplinary code be created for units which shall correspond to the war conditions." May we have page 2, please. Page 2, point 9. It says: "To establish criteria on the return of all students to the units including discontinuation of their college education until the end of the war." Do you know that a lot of young people appeared to enroll in university courses in order to -- not to have the duty to defend the territory of the HR HB? They registered fictitiously.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they actually registered or not, but I know that a large number of them did apply for university courses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it -- it goes on to say that at the level of the municipality everybody used the influence they could wield, and they would go before medical commissions to be classed as incapable for military service and thus not have to do any military service or fight.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Item 11: "Ask the government of the Republic of Croatia to revoke all refugees from municipalities of Herceg-Bosna from their refugee identifications in order to be returned to brigades." Do you know that people simply transferred to Croatia, registered themselves as refugees?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were no longer concerned in the least about whether they were liable for military service in the republic of Croatia and Herzegovina and the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, because both the ABiH and the HVO were regular units of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct? Do you have that information yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I only would like to ask you if this point 11, when it says that you are asking the government of the Republic of Croatia to revoke -- excuse me, to revoke all refugees from municipalities of Herceg-Bosna from the refugee identifications in order to be returned to brigades compositions, I wonder if this kind of demand or asking the government would have been in conflict with the rules to be applied internationally on refugees or on other people, because I really feel that -- that if a refugee left his or her country and would like to stay for well-established reasons, then probably it is a bit too much to ask for the government to revoke their kind of certification and permission to stay in their country. So I wonder if that issue was considered. And although the witness answered to this question after you asked him, "Do you have that information yourself," he said that, "Yes, I do," but then in this case probably that was a kind of cooperation between the government of the Republic of Croatia and your government and leadership. So it is my question if you consider this issue for revoking the permissions as legally established. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Judge Prandler, here it says not to refugees but refugees who are liable for military service. So we're talking about deserters, not about refugees. No one touched the refugees. Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia had an agreement at the time on military cooperation and an agreement on military cooperation -- the agreement on military cooperation signed by Tudjman and Izetbegovic also provided for the fact that a deserter in one country can't be considered as a refugee in another country. That's what item 11 is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, do you agree with what I have said?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we are discussing men who are liable for military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at item 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I only would like to ask -- the witness has confirmed that meaning, but on the other hand, at least in the English translation, there is no mentioning of a kind of -- those who are deserters, but it says, "demand from the government," et cetera, "to revoke all refugees from municipalities," and it is only in the end it is said that, "in order to be returned to brigades' compositions," but it could be interpreted in a way that they were not members of the brigade before. But anyway, you wanted to include them and to -- to draw them into the military brigades after -- when they returned. But anyway, I took -- I took, in a way, into consideration what both the witness and the Accused Praljak said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment: The English translation is faulty. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask the translators, the interpreters to precisely interpret item 11. Could General Biskic read it out?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Demand that the government of the Republic of Croatia revoke the status of refugees for all refugees who are liable for military service if they're from the municipality of Herceg-Bosna, and they should be sent back to brigades in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, this is very clear now. People liable for military service who fled from HR HB brigades, is that how we should interpret item 11?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understand the item, and I know this is a problem that did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on to item 13. "Show no mercy when dealing with the black market and crime, and urgently take the following measures: Have -- hold a meeting with all the chiefs of the SIS; have identical criteria for the work of the civil police, the military police, the active forces, and the brigade military police in all SIS services; create regulation codes on establishment of military police, create the regulation code for the work of the border police," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was forwarded to the Prime Minister, the minister of defence, and the command of the HVO Main Staff. And have a look at the signatories. Do you know these commanders of brigades and of military districts, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we scroll up, please. Scroll up, please. It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the names now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you know these people on the whole?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them. I know almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you come across the same problems? Did you try to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now have a look at the following document -- or, rather, I have something else I would like to raise. At a meeting in Zagreb that you had on the 6th of November, 1993 were such problems analysed? Were you informed of the nature of the problems that existed down there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not perhaps to this extent, but problems that concerned the Uskoplje area in Central Bosnia were discussed, and according to what General Tole said, one could draw the conclusion that there were in fact many problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were you aware of the fact that General Tole, the chief of my HVO staff at the time, was in Zagreb, although I was unaware of the fact and had not authorised that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of these documents, can one see, and this is the conclusion you reached down there as well, that the social systems in that area were almost completely paralysed for reasons that we can't go into right now? Could we put it in this way, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in a certain sense, although I wouldn't go into giving an assessment of the civil structures, but as far as the chain of command is concerned, when we arrived there, there were many problems, and this also includes some problems that concern mobilisation, logistics, and the entire security system or providing security for a sufficient number of HVO members who were to engage in defence at the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was because of the duration of the war, the number of the dead and the wounded, the number of refugees, fear, exhaustion, despair. Is what I have just said correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were international plans and meetings that yielded no results; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact at a meeting in Split on the 5th of November, 1993, I, because of such unresolved problems, offered my resignation but also asked that Mate Boban resign because of the desperate situation? Were you aware of such information?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now see 3D 00405. 3D 00405. It's an information from SIS in Rama on an incident in Prozor. It's -- it concerns the military police. The source, SIS employees. This is what it says. The information has been checked. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you were down there in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here it says, after -- it says that Mr. Andabak had a suggestion for the new command, it says that there was a revolt on behalf -- or carried out by part of the military police. And there was a refusal to obey the new command. And then it says these people are under the leadership of Ante Baketaric. They were led by Ante Baketaric. They came to the military police building. They took charge of the radio set, weapons, ammunition, and an armed combat vehicle, and they moved all of these items to the Duga restaurant where they apparently have a new base. And then it says in that way UN passage was also blocked. The UN was passing by at the time, and the passage of a number of buses transporting soldiers to their shift on the Uskoplje battlefield was also blocked.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should scroll up so that we can see the second page of the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here it says afterwards there was an all-out shoot -- an all-out shoot-out in the town and thousands of bullets were fired and the town of Prozor was blocked. Are you familiar with this incident?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the incident. I cannot now remember all the details, but for the first two months that I spent down there we frequently had to deal with problems in Rama.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there such problems or similar problems in other parts of the HZ HB? Was there shooting, drugs? Was there looting, banditry? Were there dead people every day?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not every day in all area, but, yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't really mean every day in all places and so on, but was the number of such incidents, such problems, so significant that it wasn't possible to deal with these problems for months? We can see this on the basis of your reports too.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were gradually gaining control of the situation in December when the civil police started acting, and I think that such problems were less frequent in February, March, April, and after that period. Could we now see 3D 00113, please. 3D 00113. This is also a report from Mr. Zvonko Katovic. We will see this on the last page. He's the deputy commander for the SIS in the Tomislavgrad military district. It's addressed to the Main Staff in Posusje, and to the SIS administration in Mostar. Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's Tomislavgrad. The date is the 20th of June, 1994. And this is a report on the problems that existed, and there are dates mentioned. Unfortunately, I can't go through the whole report, but we'll first discuss the well-known event of the 25th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute before we move on. You have already used up one minute of Mr. Petkovic's time, so all the additional time you take up shall be deducted from Mr. Petkovic's time, and I believe that Mr. Petkovic only gave you seven minutes. Counsel Alaburic, how much time has the accused been granted?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we agreed on allocating General Praljak seven and a half minutes, which is what -- in fact what Mr. Praljak said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have already taken up half a minute extra, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will now conclude. I would just like to comment on this document, and then I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with the report because at the time I was no longer in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. As for the event of the 25th of February, yes, I'm familiar with that event. We discussed it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the event in which a certain Banja Luka hit and captured Colonel -- Colonel Skender in December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was in December 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see that there were two men killed here, that three tanks were taken out?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph -- or, rather, the third one. It says three tanks were brought in front of the building where the command post was located and they threatened to destroy it. Can you see that in the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're familiar with that event? Yesterday I asked you and you said that you didn't know whether they called me to assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, put your final question that relates to this document. What is it that you want the witness to tell you with regard to the contents of the document? And everyone has read the document. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many problems are referred to in this document, problems that occurred in the municipality at the time that you were present there. Are you familiar with these problems, and how much time did you need in order to bring order to just one municipality in order to gain control of just one municipality?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as Rama is concerned, it was really a municipality which required a lot of work, a lot of effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I have now concluded my cross-examination. I have now finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Biskic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic, and will address you as such, and I'm going to go through some of the things we've already heard. I shall ask you for more detailed information, and, asked by Judge Trechsel something, I don't think the answer was quite correct. So we'll deal with that. But I would like to provide their Judges with more comprehensive answer to what General Praljak asked you about the refugee ID cards for persons who were liable for military service, who were conscripts. So, Mr. Biskic, to the best your knowledge, the regulations that were in force in Herceg-Bosna at the time, did they state that men, if going abroad, must be given permission from the municipality where they were resident?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, yes, because most of the regulations were inherited from the former state, and that was an obligation that had to be fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, the request that Mr. Praljak asked you about, did it relate precisely to military conscripts who had gone to another state, the Republic of Croatia, without permission from the department of defence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Biskic, you told us that in November 1993 you came to Herceg-Bosna, and you told us that you became assistant command -- assistant chief of the Main Staff for the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning I was taken to that duty without any appointment papers. I was orally appointed, in fact, to that post.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you told us that nobody had occupied that post before you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I had been told.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that that is why there was no hand-over of duty because there were no papers, no documents, nor was there an individual whom you can take over this duty from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since in the transcript my question wasn't recorded in line 7, 8, and 9 of this page, let me repeat that it was the assistant chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. That was the title.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to correct you. There was no -- it wasn't a commander, but the chief of staff was General Ante Roso, and I was the assistant for the SIS and military police but without this establishment regulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. The -- we know that for a time the term used was the commander of the Main Staff, and later on and before that it was chief of the Main Staff. But anyway, it was the same post meaning the number one man in the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, some three weeks later you were appointed assistant minister for security.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 1st of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that in the Main Staff before you there was not -- no person dealing with military security and the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, from that period of time there was no person who performed those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that the time you spent in the Main Staff was about three weeks and that that was a sort of timeout until the regulations were compiled in the defence department and the prerequisites laid down for your appointment as assistant security minister?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can understand it that way, with the proviso that already in November I began working with Minister Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, I'd like Mr. Biskic to try and analyse how come in the Main Staff nobody before you, and I hope you'll agree, or after you for that matter, performed the security tasks within the military police. Let us take a look at the security service first. Do we agree that we use the term SIS, S-I-S, and we are thinking of the security and information service; is that right? Shall we clear that point up?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, was SIS the administration -- an administration or department in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a defence department and later a department in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And was there a head, a chief at the top of that department?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the department have its organisational centres and organisational units, which were called centres, and they were active in a part of the territory of held -- of Herceg-Bosna? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the head of that centre was the head of the centre; right? The chief?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there SIS employees in the commands of the military districts of these areas in the HVO units as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there assistant commanders in the military districts and brigades and other HVO units?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were these assistant commanders for security responsible to the superior centre or administration, and did they report back to the centre or administration about all security related matters of interest?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were supposed to report to the centres. The centres were supposed to report to the administration, and also they were duty-bound to send in reports to the commanders of the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my next question. So the commanders of units were authorised to issue orders in the area of security or counter-intelligence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in December 1993, you issued an order about competence and authority in issuing orders within SIS. It is P 07258.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we have that document up on e-court, and could the witness be provided with a set of my own documents, a bundle of my documents, please, Usher. That will facilitate our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, the document is dated the 19th of December, 1993, in which you explain the reporting to security service of the HVO, and on the basis of this document of yours we drew up a schematic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is 4D 00507, this schematic. May we place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could ask the usher to place the copy on the ELMO. The number is 4D 00507. So may we have it on the overhead projector, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, I don't want to spend too much time on the topic of SIS, discussing SIS, but I'd just like to ask you to take a look at this schematic, and document P 72 -- 07258 can compare the correctness of this schematic. And I'm asking you, Mr. Biskic, whether on that --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got it up here yet. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher can take my copy and place it on the ELMO. Usher. These are the relationships and chain of command. Can we have a look at the lower right-hand portion, because we didn't draw the diagram for each military district because the organisation was the same for all of them. So may we have a clear view of the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you tell us whether this schematic reflects the relationships within all the institutions deal with matters of security?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we need tender this as an IC document because we'll be tendering it as one of our own documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, having seen this sketch, do we agree that the Main Staff of the HVO does in the exist in the chart of the security service system?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as far as I remember, a department for security within the Main Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When was it established? In December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But it's not contained in your letter.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a surname beginning with "Ch." A gentleman whose surname began with "Ch." He was appointed to that department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I can see nothing here related to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably -- well, there are documents about the authority and powers of that department, but he probably didn't have authority -- any authority towards the centres themselves, so that this diagram can be accepted in principle, but I would be very happy if you could find that part somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that there's a document like that which says that a centre like that was established attached to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't called centre. It was called department for security or sector for security and probably it dealt with the security of the Main Staff. But as I say, I can't say that with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As it doesn't exist in your document, and there is no other document about this, can we then conclude that up until the material time in the Main Staff there was no organisational unit of SIS? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now with respect to the military police, and we're going to deal a great deal more with the military police, and I'm sure my colleagues will, too, so I'll be brief about the military police, may we take a look at a document that we discussed, and it is P 07018. It is an order of the then minister of defence about the reorganisation of the military police. P 07018 is the document number. Just briefly. May we have a look at item 4 of this order. Would you please look at it, Mr. Biskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on item 4, point 4? I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that -- I apologise, but I can't see point 4, so may we scroll down the document? Can we scroll down?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, this is in the Prosecution bundle.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can read it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It says: "The management and come -- part of the military process is done by the administration of the military police and then the assignments and task are enumerated. It establishes the basis for the development of the military police, the basis for the establishment of the military police," and it goes on to enumerate the other tasks, and it says that the military police administrations have obsolete priority in implementing the tasks assigned to them. Tell us, please, this authorisation command of the military police, does that refer to all military police units?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in points 4.3 and 4.4, we have the relationships between the military police and certain HVO unit commanders, and this is interesting from the aspects of the people from the Main Staff. And in point 4.3 it says that the commanders of the 2nd and 3rd Battalion of the military police in carrying out their daily tasks are subordinated to the commanders of the HVO military districts, and I'm skipping a sentence now, and it goes on to say, a report on the daily engagement shall be sent out to the military police administration, to the commander of the military district, to the assistant commander for SIS in the military district, to the military prosecutor, the military court judge, and the MUP police administration. Tell me, Mr. Biskic, from this provision it would emerge that the Main Staff is not in the chain of command vis-a-vis the 2nd and 3rd Battalion of the military police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Main Staff is in the chain of command towards the military districts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm asking you about the battalions of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right. There's no logic that this should be in that particular chain of command, if we're going to speak about the hierarchy of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff similarly in -- is not in the reporting chain.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind you of what we said yesterday. We looked at a bulletin yesterday, and so in that sense daily reports were sent to the Main Staff of the HVO as well, because reference is made here to the daily report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But there's no mention of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the level of the administration of the military police then all the reports are collected together and the bulletin was sent to the chief of the Main Staff as well. I'd like to remind you of bulletin number 2 that we discussed, I think yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So may we now conclude that these are individual reports, so individual reports do not go to the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Not as such, but in a processed form, a daily report for all the areas of responsibility of military police units, from the 17th of November they did receive them, and I do believe that this was -- reporting was similar prior to that. But as of that date they did receive reports on daily engagement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, let's clarify what we mean by collective reports and individual reports so that we avoid any misunderstanding. I don't think that there is any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't. I think we're speaking -- talking about same thing and I'll try and explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, there's no need because we seem to be spending too much time on this and I have more important topics to deal with. So please tell me now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If they could slow down a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic, you're not wasting time. What you're saying is very important, and this leads me to ask a question, and I have to ask this question. General, the Petkovic Defence team is asking you if, in the chain of command, according to the chain of command, the Main Staff, which at the time was helped by General Roso, but before that was headed by General Petkovic, was within the chain of command concerning military police matters, and the Defence counsel maintains that it is not. Now, it would appear from your answers that on several occasions you indicated that it was kept abreast of the situation through reports, and now the Defence is distinguishing between general reports and individual reports. But in looking at this particular document, I can observe, and I'd like you to help me out here and tell me your position, on the 3rd of December the minister of defence sends out an order to everybody on the fact that the military police battalions were engaged, the 1st Battalion Mostar, the 2nd in Livno, et cetera, et cetera. And following on from what you suggest - and this is marked in the document - we see here that it says, "With the agreement of General Roso." Now, I want to understand this. If General Roso was not in this chain of command, why did you ask for his agreement? On the other hand, if he was in the chain of command, then we could understand that your suggestion was also submitted to him for his approval. Can you see in B/C/S the version of the document? It says, "With the agreement of General Roso." It's in the document. So ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- Your Honour, I have understood your question. Naturally the chief of the Main Staff agreed to the new establishment of the military police. The chief of the Main Staff is in command of all the units of the HVO. The chief of the Main Staff has no reason to directly command the battalions of military police. He can do so through military districts. And every order of the chief of the Main Staff that was forwarded to me in order to engage additional military police forces, well, naturally I thought such an order was binding, in my opinion. As far as the system of reporting is concerned, there were daily reports. Units would send reports to the military police administration. They'd compile a summary report and forward the summary report to all the addresses we discussed yesterday or the day before yesterday. When we were discussing the bulletin of the military police, that's -- that concerns daily engagement. As far as specific tasks, though, that are concerned, that they would receive from commanders of military districts, well, naturally, given the line of reporting, if the commander of a military district received a report, it was his duty to inform the main command, especially if there was something of interest. And in this way the chief of the Main Staff would receive information. It would be through the daily reports of individual units. I'm talking about the period during which I was present down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Counsel Alaburic, do continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll continue from where I stopped off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, if I'm not mistaken, we agreed that the Main Staff is not in the direct chain of command with respect to the military police. It's not a part of the system of reporting as far as individual reports are concerned, but they would receive a collective summary report from the military police administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as the agreement of the chief of the Main Staff is concerned, tell me, Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with the former rules on the organisation and reorganisation of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to an extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in any of those documents and at any time, did you see a signature that represented someone's agreement of the chief -- or, rather, the agreement of the chief -- or, rather, the agreement of the chief of the Main Staff or the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that, but I must explain something to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in whether you saw this or not.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We are interested, Witness. If you have something to explain, please do explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that I have nothing against the witness explaining this, but I would then be grateful if the -- his answer wasn't deducted from my time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to explain that this order was in a certain sense an order that regulated the system of command at the time. There was a new structure. And after this order there were these booklets that were compiled in the department for the structuring of the HVO. I can't remember who did it. And then there was a new rule book on the work of the military police that was signed by the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And previously there was also a rule book on the work of the military police of the HVO. It was April 1993, I think, and there were these booklets I have mentioned. So this order, in a certain sense, when these booklets and rules came into force -- well, in a certain sense you could say that these -- this order was subsequently put into those two documents, into the booklet, and the rule book of the military police at the time that -- chief of the Main Staff did not express his agreement with regard to this matter. That's what I wanted to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, in 1993 was the military police in the Republic of Croatia organised in a more or less similar way?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in an almost identical way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that today in the Republic of Croatia the military police within the main -- is within the Main Staff of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer will be yes, but at different times the military police was structured in a different way in the armed forces the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we can move on to another subject that concerns detention centres and taking people out to perform labour, detainees out to perform labour. Mr. Biskic, we have seen minutes from meetings recently, meetings that were held in order to implement the order of the late President Mate Boban, an order of the 10th of December, 1993 that concerns disbanding all detention centres. And if I have read it correctly, at those meetings there were no representatives of the Main Staff present.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the HVO Main Staff had no authority to establish or disband collection -- or, rather, detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know who was authorised, and I didn't see the exact contents of the decision of the president of Herceg-Bosna on disbanding these centres. So that's the only answer I could provide to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the HVO Main Staff had no authority to appoint or dismiss wardens of individual detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a precise answer to that question either, because I didn't see any decisions. I didn't see who would sign such decisions that concerned wardens. As far as the Heliodrom is concerned, I think it was the military police administration that was responsible, but I never saw such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me for interrupting you. General, I would like only to ask you, you said before, and I believe again you repeated, that, "I can't give you a precise answer," you said to the counsel to that question, "if only because I didn't see any decisions." And again before that you also mentioned that you didn't know the content of the decision which was actually promulgated by President Boban. Now, I am a bit surprised, because yesterday you have taken note of -- you took note of a document about a meeting which you yourself convened, and you have been there and you explain that it was a meeting about the implementation of the presidential decision. So I wonder if -- if I see here a problem here that you had to be aware what the decision was and what was the background. So I wonder if you would enlighten me about this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand your question. There's no problem as far as my answer concerns. Yesterday I really did say that I hadn't seen a written decision. I hadn't seen the contents of such a decision. I didn't know who was bound by this decision. Mr. Jukic designated me as the person responsible for disbanding those collection centres. That's what I said yesterday, and I'm repeating this today. And secondly, I didn't see a single decision on appointing wardens of the previous collection centres apart from the fact that I on the 8th of December, 1993, issued an order according to which there should be a -- Mr. Stanko Bozic as an acting officer for the company for collection centres. So I was implementing a decision of the president of Herceg-Bosna, but I didn't see this decision in its written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe I can be of assistance. The decision is really simple. There is one sentence. It's quite simple. "All the collection centres should be disbanded," and that's perhaps why this order wasn't copied. It was simply necessary to find a way in which this decision could be implemented. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, I'm asking you about the period up until your arrival, if you have any information about this; if not, you can just say so and then we can move on. Did you ever see a decision of any kind or notes of any kind according to which the Main Staff was establishing the rules of procedure in a detention centre of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, the house rules. Did you ever see a decision or notes according to which the Main Staff was to participate in categorising people who had been deprived of their liberty?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw such an a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we discussed Prosecution document P 07075. Mr. Biskic, this is your letter dated the 18th of December, 1993, a letter on -- establishing a military police company to provide security for centre for POWs. The date is the 8th of December, not the 18th, as it says in the transcript. And there is one sentence in that letter of yours that I'm particularly interested in. "I hereby forbid without approval of the security service prisoners from being taken out to perform labour." Sir, tell me, did you -- or, rather, did your sector have the authority to issue permission to take detainees out to perform labour? Did you have such authority?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have such authority. The chief of the Main Staff would authorise individuals in his orders. He quite precisely stated who had such authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is the legal basis for order issued by General Roso? Can you tell me that? And how was it possible for General Roso to order you to do anything as the deputy minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that General Roso issued an order to me. General Roso issued an order to all HVO units, according to which it was forbidden to take detainees out from collection centres, and he ordered that all those who had been taken out of collection centres should be returned to them. But since you have asked me a question about the letter dated the 8th of December, and since the military police security to provide -- that was designated to provide security for a collection centre was under the military police, and under my sector, by virtue of that fact, I stated in that item of my letter that I was making Mr. Bozic also responsible to inform the sector of the letters he had received and that referred to the order issued by the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, would you agree with me that the chief of the Main Staff, Mr. Roso, had no authority over the Heliodrom, but he did have authority over HVO units?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the chief of the Main Staff can forbid his units to take detainees out to perform labour, but he cannot order the Heliodrom administration to act in any way when it comes to taking detainees out to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on how we interpret the chain of command. In practice things were somewhat different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the chain of command. Could the chief of the Main Staff issue an order of any kind to the prison warden -- or, rather, to the warden of the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he issued any such order, but if he had issued it, it would certainly have been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now interested in legal matters. Was he in a position to issue such orders? Did he have such authority? Do you agree that he did not have the authority to issue such orders to the Heliodrom warden or to the warden of any other collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have already say, if the chief of the Main Staff had ordered me to asked forces to the military police in any part of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, I would have carried out the order. I wouldn't have asked myself whether he had the authority to issue such orders or not, because it was a state of the war and it was also a matter of implementing an order of someone who was at the head of the HVO, and this is how we acted in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. For the sake of the interpreters, may I ask you to slow down and to have a pause between your questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, in order for you to abide by such an order issued by General Roso -- well, I understand what you have said, but what we are interested in right now is the actual legal relationship between the chief of the Main Staff, and in this specific case the deputy minister, and we're interested in the authority for the -- that General Roso might have to act in a certain way, the authority he has on a legal basis.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had no such legal basis to act, because I was not in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well so we do agree as far as that is concerned. Now, let us discuss an answer you gave to a question put to you yesterday by Judge Trechsel, I believe. Judge Trechsel asked you the following: If the Heliodrom warden had good grounds to believe that prisoners would be taken out to perform labour at the front line, could he have refused the request to hand other detainees to perform labour? Your answer was he couldn't refuse to do this if there was authorisation from an authorised official. Is that answer correctly quoted?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, at the time of the former Yugoslavia and right up until the present in all the countries of the former Yugoslavia, do you remember whether the rules on the armed forces established that a member of the military who received an order to act in a criminal way could refuse to act in such a way?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My answer is yes, but let me go back to the previous explanation I provided you with, because we are now trying to guess whether Stanko Bozic could have been aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel posed a very precise and definite question. He said: "If he had good reason to believe that those prisoners would be taken up to the front line." So it wasn't guesswork. It was a probability. And in view of previous experience, perhaps the certain knowledge that this would happen. So now the question was: Could the warden have refused to let those detainees be taken out. Do you wish to correct your answer, reconsider?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't want to consider my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, do we agree that criminal codes of the SFRY to the present day in Croatia, and indeed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, establish the right of a subordinate to refuse to carry out an order from his superior if they consider it to be a serious crime, and especially if they would consider it to be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case today and that was always the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you consider that prison wardens belong to some sort of hierarchical chain of responsibility and relationship to the Main Staff or the Ministry of Defence or any other institution, for that matter, whose member could demand that detainees be taken out to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your question. Could you repeat it please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that somebody can issue an order to somebody else, somebody superior -- somebody subordinate to him in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in that sense, to whom was the warden subordinate to? Be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you were there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Mr. Lavric, the acting person of the 22nd of November, it was the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was any HVO unit able then to issue an order to the warden of the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we remember that the order from General Milivoj Petkovic of October, we said that without permission from the Main Staff detainees could be -- could not be taken out to perform labour. All I can say is that the practice was that, if this came from the Main Staff, then the warden of Heliodrom automatically complied with the order, but I'm guessing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, wouldn't it be proper, faced with a situation of that kind, to call this, "request to be given prisoners" instead of an order? Can we term it a "request"? Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how the warden took this. I can agree with you; however, I cannot say what the warden thought, so I can't tell you what the warden had in mind and thought about this at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that the letters -- the documents were titled "request" or things like that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I can't answer this because I didn't see the documents which made the request.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Regardless of practice and regardless of the fact that it wouldn't enter anybody's mind not to comply with a request made by someone, in the formal and legal sense would the warden of Heliodrom be authorised to prevent detainees being taken out to perform labour, if he thought they would be taken out to the front line?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer I gave yesterday I gave using concrete examples because I never saw somebody take them where they were forbid to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, Mr. Biskic, about what actually happened. I'm asking you about authorisation, along the lines of Judge Trechsel. Could the warden had done this if he had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably he could have. Now, what the repercussions would have been, I don't know, but I assume that he could have. Had I been in his place, that's probably how I would have acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know of any situations in which the -- with the change of the warden of a detention centre the situation in the centre changed drastically, including this matter of prisoners being taken out to perform labour, thanks to this new number-one man in the prison, the new warden?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no experience in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me now, please, Mr. Biskic, you and your collaborators who came to Herceg-Bosna at that time and together with everybody else who was there at the time invested great efforts to enforce efficient and effective control over whether people were taken out to do labour or not, and you encountered a great deal of difficulty, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a -- problems related to their return were also very serious, as well as them being taken out in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. And I'm sure one of my colleagues will ask you about that so I'd like to move on to another area, and that is the relationship between the civilian authorities and the military units, in general terms. Now, in the minutes from a meeting of the offices of the military police dated the 14th of December, 1993, and this was Prosecution document P 07169, the following was recorded, your words, that the municipal brigades were being disbanded and that they were moving to a unified salary list so that somebody could not receive a salary regularly, whereas somebody else had not received a salary for three months. And this is quotation which is on page 10 of the B/C/S text, and it is on page 23 of the English. Do you remember that? Do you remember saying that, Mr. Biskic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw that in the transcript, and I think that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you meant by a municipal brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said yesterday that some of the brigades of the Croatian Defence Council were financed by the municipalities. There was no uniform payment of salaries, and I attended meetings discussing that issue because in some places in December the system of paying out salaries from the defence ministry had started, and also at discussions at meetings with respect to reporting from commanders and military districts, it was noted that individual brigades were receiving their salaries on a regular basis, whereas others had not received them for several months, so that these municipal brigades -- well, that wasn't their official title and name, but they were in part under the auspices, if I can put it that way, of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you arrived in Herceg-Bosna, did you come across a situation by which this problem had been evidenced and that steps had been taken to resolve it, or did you discover the problem?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the problem existed beforehand and that they were doing their best to try and solve it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's why I would like us to look at a document together now. It is 4D 00508.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that this one here?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is 4D 00508, and they are the minutes from a government meeting of the HR HB held on the 9th of October, 1993. The subject was the military security situation, and reports were submitted by Minister Stojic and Generals Praljak and Petkovic. And we can see that they dealt critically with the functioning of the civilian authorities, and in the second paragraph they say that -- they pointed out the adverse consequences of the inconsistent application of rules and regulations and the voluntariness in conduct on the part of the civilian authorities in individual municipalities which affected the combat readiness and morale of the soldiers and the functioning of a unified financial system, which had a negative effect on securing the same materiel position for all of the armed forces. So is this the same problem that you noticed and tried to solve?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us see what the government tried to do to solve the problem. And among other things, in point 2 it says that proposals will be made to the house of representatives to enact regulations which would regulate relationships between the central and local authorities, and, due to wartime circumstances, that the authority would be centralised. And then based on a unified financial system we must secure payments into the HR HB budget, and so on. Tell us now, please, Mr. Biskic, and this is something that General Praljak asked you about, and it's a very important question for us, this system of financing, did it strengthen the influence of the municipal officials on the HVO units which were active on the territory of individual municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, for that reason, the effective control of any central organ including the Main Staff, was it significantly diminished because of that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see that the time has come for us to take a break, so if we continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is 10 to 4.00 almost, and we'll reconvene at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Counsel Alaburic, you have 22 minutes left, or 21 minutes and 60 seconds to be exact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I see that my last question on page 42, line 7 and 8 wasn't fully recorded, so I'd like to repeat my question. It related to the financing system of the brigade at the level of the municipalities and whether this system strengthened the position of the municipal officials and their influence on the military units which were active on the territory of individual municipalities. That was my question, and the answer was, "Yes, of course, yes, certainly."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Biskic, for the record?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, as we're looking at the minutes of the extraordinary government meeting, can we look at the last point which relates to preventing crime, crime prevention. And I would like to ask you the following in that regard, Mr. Biskic: Were there any complaints from citizens about the conduct of members of the armed forces? Did the public complain?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any concrete examples, but in general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested in hearing whether the Croat population complained about certain adverse conduct on the part of the armed forces, whether under the effects of alcohol or for some other reason engaged in impermissible acts.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly, no, but judging by SIS and military police reports there were complaints of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now a few words, Mr. Biskic, in view of your enormous military experience, to help us understand some things that happened in Herceg-Bosna better. If I understood you correctly, you said you knew that the HVO -- or, rather, the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna began to be established in April 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge about that dates from that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree then that this was a period when there were war conflicts with the army of Republika Srpska and the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And after that -- or, rather, at the same time conflicts erupted with the BH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And we could conclude that in fact the army of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, was created exclusively under wartime conditions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, you arrived in Herceg-Bosna in November 1993, which means about a year and a half after the army of Herceg-Bosna had been established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
