utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Biskic, from military literature and perhaps based on your own experience as well, do you know of any case, any instance, whereby an army was created under wartime conditions and that in the space of a year from its inception or when the official decision was taken about its establishment that it was able to function according to the book and according to the rules and regulations that apply to an organised army with a long-standing tradition? Would that -- could that have been expected, with firm hierarchal relationships and everything else, of an army in a democratic country?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what the main problems were in establishing an army in wartime, and what was realistically possible when establishing that army and exerting control over that army? Or let me try and be more precise. Is it possible in such a short space of time under wartime conditions with a great many refugees, a very long front line, financial problems, problems in mobilising the citizens, and the many other problems that -- many of which were raised by General Praljak, was it possible to have an army over which a commander or commanders, including the Main Staff, really had effective control at all times in all places over every soldier?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Biskic, please, army law, a legislation, can you have all this legislation and the appointment of judges and so on, and the very next day to have military courts which would function in the kind of way that this functions in a normal, stable country which is at peace?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to how much time is needed for a legal system and legislation to begin to function in keeping with rules and regulations that apply in democratic countries?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that kind of experience. I can't answer. Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any experience in that area, so it would be difficult for me to say how much time would be needed for that to take effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if something is not clear, I was referring to military law, and that's why Judge Trechsel wanted to interfere -- intervene. It wasn't recorded clearly enough, but the witness answered with respect to the functioning of the legal system and the justice system as it applies to the army. Mr. Biskic, do you have any experience and can you make any comparison with the organisation of the army and legislation under wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that this is an area that I have not studied, so it's difficult for me to stay, but I know that all armies established at wartime required a long time for all the systems to be established and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a commander or any other official in the army or in -- the authorities in wartime conditions, when there is the danger of having individual parts of the country being controlled by an enemy army, that his primary efforts should be geared towards preventing that from happening, that is to say to keep control of the territory and preserve the entity that they are defending, or would it be his primary task to attempt on the territory that they have under control to take legal proceedings against some criminal acts? If you were faced with an alternative, would it be logical to expect commanders to deal with the first task in hand and almost exclusively so?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you explained how you arrived in Herceg-Bosna and how you were engaged, and you referred to your interview with the OTP, and you said there were so many problems and so many tasks that you had to carry out that you were unable to worry about the past. You had to deal with the present problems and establish a basis for the future. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree if I said that such rules were established and such priorities that were established also applied to the period before your arrival and especially concerned the period of the most intense war combat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And to conclude, there is one other thing I would like to ask you about. In the spring of 1994, General Roso went away from the Main Staff. Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Roso went to the Joint Staff of the HVO and the ABiH in Sarajevo. I think it was April.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was then appointed as the chief of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, that was in the spring of 1994. Isn't that correct? In April?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was that a time when it was necessary to implement the Washington Agreement and also the military agreement on peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was signed in Split on the 12th of March of that same year and it became an integral part of the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have now concluded my cross-examination. I just need to provide you with one explanation since I still have a little time left. I would like to thank my colleague, Daryl Mundis, who informed me of the documents that he wanted to tender, although he hadn't presented them to the witness, Biskic. I prepared part of my cross on the basis of that -- on -- I prepared for my cross-examination on the basis of those documents, but as these documents won't be tendered, I will conclude now. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Counsel. The Judges have a question to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question, Mr. Biskic, which refers to the interrogatory -- to the cross-examination by General Praljak, and it relates to document 3D 00796. I did not want to interrupt at the time, but -- so it comes a bit late now. Can you find that? It is in the -- the file that was at your disposal when General Praljak questioned you. This is the document dated 26th of October, with the many problems, and there in number 9 it is said, "set the unique criteria on return of all students to units, all students to units." In number 11 reference is made to Herceg-Bosna, or Bosnia and Herceg -- no, Herceg-Bosna, but here it really says, "all students." How is this to be explained? Is this some kind of -- of Croatian mobilisation that takes effect, or is it simply an omission to say that it should only refer to students in some relation with Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can't answer that question. I think that General Praljak can certainly answer the question. I don't know whether they're referring to students in the Republic of Croatia who are from Bosnia and Herzegovina or perhaps from Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Praljak is not at this moment a witness here, so if that ever should happen, I will come back with a question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I could be of assistance. You could remind perhaps the witness at the time there was not a single university in the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, at that time. There was one in Neum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now for the next Defence team. You have 75 minutes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know you're looking at me in that way because you have a very fat binder before you, but these voluminous documents, but I will only quote certain parts from the documents, and I think I'll have some minutes left if my client believes he needs to put additional questions to the witness. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll be dealing with the military police on the whole since I'm defending Valentin Coric in this case. I assume you understand why I will be dealing with this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, could you speak a little closer to the microphone. Could you approach the microphone since the interpreters are having some difficulty hearing you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Can they hear me now? Is this all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to go back to the time of your arrival in Herceg-Bosna and the role you played when you assumed your duties in the Ministry of Defence. We've already heard about this. There was a security sector in the ministry of defence within which there was the military police administration and the SIS administration. When you became the deputy defence minister on the 1st of December, 1993, you were simultaneously the chief of the security sector. It follows that you also the superior of -- you also, the superior of the chief of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I became the deputy minister I was the superior of the chief of military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I want to go back to the time before your arrival. I know that you have already told us that you weren't precisely familiar with all the events, but you'd nevertheless gathered quite a lot of information. So I would like to go through some documents that concern the structure of the defence department, which preceded the Ministry of Defence de facto and de jure. Could we see P 00586 on the screen, please. That is document that concerns -- P 00586. This is a document on the structure of the defence department. 18th of October, 1992 is the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 17th, interpreter's correction. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in items IV and V. It's the third page in the Croatian version and in the English. I'll now read through the part I'm interested in. It says, "for certain sectors the head will have assistance. Item I, assistant for the head of security." I'm only interested in this at the moment because that is the sector I'm interested in. Item V says: "The deputy head for security shall be responsible for the security section which shall encompass the SIS and the military police administration. The deputy for security shall also perform the duties of the chief of the security administration." This decision shows that within the then defence department there was a deputy security officer who was responsible for the security sector, and it also included the SIS administration and the military police administration. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that according to this structure the deputy for security would be superior to the chief of the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item V says the deputy head for security is at the same time the chief of the security administration. When we have a look at this structure, does the deputy for security at the time of the existence of the defence department have the same duties and responsibilities, given his position, as those that you had subsequently in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we have a look at this decision, yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look to document P 02477, and it concerns the structure that was established at a somewhat later date, a decision on the internal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Before -- before we leave this document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, do you know, Mr. Biskic, whether in fact there was a deputy head for security before you were there in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I have already said, I wasn't assigned my duties by anyone. When I arrived, there were the chiefs of the SIS administration and of the military police administration, but no one introduced himself to me as the deputy head for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have -- certainly you have found certain documents at least. Have you ever come upon any trace of someone having held the function that on paper existed? Did you have any trace of this? Did someone tell you about this? You must have inquired. It's the natural reaction that you say, "Who did this before me?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I have already said, when I arrived down there I was initially the deputy chief of the Main Staff for security within the military police. Later, in the course of discussions in November, I took over the role of an assistant, and as of the 1st of December I actually or really took over these duties. I didn't come across a single document, nor did anyone tell me that Mr. Ivica Lucic, who was the chief of the SIS administration, acted as the deputy head for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I wanted to see P 02477 on the screen. It's a decision on the internal organisation of the defence department dated the 20th of May, 1993. P 02477. Under A I'll read out item number II, which reads as follows: "Assistant heads for sectors the defence department manage the work for their sectors and are responsible for it in accordance with the guidelines issued by the head of the defence department and the established work programme." And now I would like to have a look at the following item, the next item, IV, item IV under B. It's the end of the second page and the beginning of the third page in the English version, and it reads always follows. I'll just read out one sentence that is important to me: "Within the security sector we shall also find the military police administration as a component." I'd just like to note that the defence department wasn't changed by this new structure, at least not as far as its component parts were concerned. I won't go into any other details. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, when he was the chief of the SIS, from the time the department was established and right up until his arrival he played that role?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was from the beginning, but I knew about a certain period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's throughout 1993. As for whether it was also the case prior to that date, I don't know, but I assume he was there from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that in the course of your work you dealt with the structure and situation in the military police, and you mentioned the problems that the military police encountered in the course of its operations. I've heard some things about it in the course of your examination-in-chief, and I found out other things from your interview with the investigators. I'd just like to mention some problems that I noted in your presentation. They concern problems as far as being engaged at the front lines is concerned, the problems that concern coordination of the work of the Ministry of the Interior and the SIS, the MUP and the SIS, and also the problem of failing to understand the chain of command and authority of the military police and of various HVO commanders. Do you remember all of these matters?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the documents and deal with this period by period. These are documents that have already been shown in the courtroom, and they should assist us to deal with the matter more thoroughly. And I also think this is an excellent opportunity for me to adequately examine all these documents now. Could we now have the following document on the screen: P 00128. It's a report on the work of the HVO in 1992. Page 7 in the Croatian version, page 5 in the English version. Item III is the one we're interested in. It concerns the situation in districts. "Defence," second paragraph -- or, rather, first. I'll read out the first sentence first paragraph. It says: "The defence department of the HVO HZ HB was officially established at a session of the Presidency of the HZ HB on the 15th of May, 1992." And then I'll move on to the first sentence in the following paragraph. Structural organisation and work in this sphere in practice began with the -- with the appointment of the head of the defence department on the 3rd of July, 1992." Am I correct to draw the conclusion that this shows that the defence department - and the military police administration was part of it - in fact started being structured and started operating on the 3rd of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you're asking me a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This report was compiled out of reports from various HVO departments, different departments of the HVO, and I'd like to go through some points that are important to me. May we first take a look in the Croatian version page 11, and in English it is on page 8, the paragraph begins on page 8 and then goes on to page 9. It's the last paragraph. It is part of the report relating to the functioning of SIS. It says: "A separate problem was the limited work of the civilian police, functioning of the civilian police and the MUP organs, and the lack of functioning on the part of the judiciary. So functioning in certain situations was limited and determined by these factors, which had a considerable influence on effectiveness in individual cases. In that respect, contacts were established with representatives of the departments for the interior with the aim of overcoming the ensuing problems and misunderstandings, especially with regard to the competence and authority in the work of the services mentioned." Am I right in concluding that this reflects the problems that you encountered when you took up your post in the HZ HB, which was later to be the HR HB, and this was reflected in the work of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that, but I can't see that on page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm reading it on e-court, but I'll tell you the number on the hard copy, and on the hard copy it's on page 9. I'd like to move on now. Let's move on to the next page. It is page 9 of the English, last paragraph. Last paragraph of page 9 and then continues on to page 10. And in the Croatian version it is page 12, and it says number 10 in -- on the hard copy, and this relates to the military police. It says the following: "Commands of the operative groups were established and a Joint Command of the military police administration was formed; however, territorial obstacles and war conflicts in certain areas, particularly in Bosanska Posavina and some parts of Central Bosnia, have prevented the establishment of functional links between all military police units despite all efforts." In the transcript of your interview with the OTP I found that you had problems with this functional link and the poor contacts with Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So is this what the situation was like on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move down two paragraphs -- or, rather, we're skipping one paragraph and going on to the next one, second sentence. "Since military police stations have not been adequately enough staffed to prevent crime, efforts have been made to act in the sphere of crime in cooperation with the Ministry of Interior organs." Tell me, do you know that the military police units encountered problems with staffing at that time and the technical resources?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of cooperation at that time along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can I conclude from this paragraph that efforts were made as far as was possible to cooperate in that area, too, with the Ministry of the Interior? And I assume we're dealing with the civilian police here.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I also assume that what is referred to is the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to page 13, and it is page 11, second paragraph of the English version, and your page 11 too. And we begin with the second sentence of that paragraph, which says: "In the course of September, reorganisation was undertaken of the military police administration and the military police units so that as of the 1st of October, 1992, within the frameworks of its competencies and remit, the military police has operated in accordance with new organisational schemes regulated by the instructions for the work of the military police of the HVO HZ HB. The military police administration is organised through the department of general and traffic military police and the crime prevention department." From what I've read, I conclude that the crime prevention department within the military police was established and started working on the basis of this new establishment on the 1st of October, 1992. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, may we go on to page 15 of the Croatian text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have a -- I have a question about the -- but I have pressed it all right. I have problems with understanding, what is the meaning of "is organised through the department of general and traffic military police"? "Organised through," I do not understand the meaning of this. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the witness will agree with me, but I believe the military police organisation was composed of departments one of which was the general and traffic military police and the other department was the crime prevention department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Am I right witness?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we now have page 15 of the Croatian version which is page 13 of the English version, first paragraph, and the third paragraph in the Croatian version, and I'm reading it. "Apart from the activities mentioned within the frameworks of its competence and authority, the military police units on several occasions became involved at combat up at the front line. The members of the military police in such cases perform all their combat assignments successfully. Going about their duties from the beginning of the war to the present day, eight members of the military police laid down their lives, and 48 members of the military police were wounded, whether seriously or less seriously." Now, I assume that what I've just read out is in conformity with what you said about the involvement of the military police up at the front line. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It testifies to continuity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct that when the military police was engaged up at the front line that this in a way handicapped them -- was a handicap in performing their regular police tasks otherwise, which, in view of their numbers, was made more difficult, or when the units came back from the battlefield they suffered from fatigue and weren't able to go about their normal daily duties. Am I right there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we now have the next part of the document on our screens. In Croatian it is page 21. It is your page 19, and in English it is page 18, the last paragraph. In the Croatian version, I'm going to read the second paragraph. We've already been through this document, so I'm just going to briefly tell you what it's about. It describes the tasks and assignments of the civilian police, what they did, and towards the middle of the paragraph we can see that they also dealt withal solving crimes, war crimes, genocide, classical forms of crime, and so on. So I think that we can agree that those are all things that the civilian police deals with.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we now move on to the next page. In English it is on page 19, third paragraph. In the Croatian version it is the first paragraph of page 21, and I would like to read the penultimate sentence there which says the following: "The age structure of the perpetrators of crimes in this area indicates that it was persons from the ages of 25 to 30 who perpetrate crimes of this kind, and they were individuals who at the time they committed the offences wore uniforms." It's your page -- on your page 20, the penultimate sentence. And then let's move on to the next page. It is your page 21. On e-court it is page 23, and for the English it is on page 20. It is the fourth paragraph in English and third in the Croatian, and it states as follows: "Armed combat in the area and all its implications --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just note that our version of the text does not contain any reference to wearing of uniforms. Maybe it's a mistake in the translation, but I think you should know that. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'll check that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While you check, maybe I may ask a question to the witness. Witness, we have heard several times of the engagement of military police at the front line. This is a problem. Can you tell us who was responsible for this? Who sent military police to the front line? Did the military commanders order them or request for their assistance, or did the military police take the initiative? Do you know how this came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the military police cannot take the initiative on its own. This was pursuant to a request or command by a commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And do you think that the military police authorities could not refuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you recall, Your Honour, my answer to General Praljak, I said everything depended on the situation. If the situation was such that there was nobody to defend the front line, then of course all forces should be included for the defence of the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Judge Trechsel is quite right. In the English version, that word has indeed been omitted about the uniforms, but you can look at the original text, and you can see that I read out what it said. So I'm sorry that the translation there is faulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I trust you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] It is a Prosecution document, so I didn't think I need check it, but you can check the Croatian version, the original. The next page I'd like to look at is page 23 in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, it is on your page 21. And in the English it is on page 20, paragraph 4. "The armed combat that has taken place in this area and all its implications have undoubtedly been reflected in the sphere of crime as manifested in the uncontrolled violation of the law by the commission of all sorts of offences. To a considerable extent this has been favoured by the non-functioning of the rule of law and of some police stations and by numerous and widespread crimes committed by uniformed persons." Tell me, please, would this description of the situation as provided by the department of the interior be a realistic rendition of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's partially the situation that I encountered when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So if we look at this it, then we can see that the civilian police dealt with crimes perpetrated by persons in uniform. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we now look at page 30? It is your page 28, and in English it is page 27, second paragraph. In the Croatian version it is the fourth and last paragraph, and it relates to the legal system and the administration, and I'm reading out the first sentence which says: "Provisions on the establishment of military legal system was undertaken, and at a meeting of the 17th of October, 1992, a provision was passed on military district courts and district military prosecutors' offices." Now, when the military police deals with crimes, its role - that's my conclusion - is reduced to filing criminal reports, uncovering the perpetrators, bringing them to justice. In this instance, the military prosecutor's office and then to the military courts for the military. In other words, for the military police to be able to perform its work successfully and to prevent crime and to bring the perpetrators to justice, this would require military judicial bodies and the military legal system to function properly.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From what I've read out here, we can see that the provision to establish military judiciary bodies and district military courts was passed on the 7th of October, 1992, as late as that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to another period and area, so may we have on e-court document P 04699 next, please. And it is once again an HVO report, this time for the period from January to June 1993. Page 20 in the Croatian version. It is on page 18 for you, and page 12 for the English, second paragraph, and it is the third paragraph in the Croatian version. This concerns the activities of the SIS administration at the time, and I'll read out the sentence: "The service registered a number of crimes at the same time committed by members of the HVO both in the territory of Central Bosnia and in the territory of Mostar, as well as in other municipalities." We can see that the SIS was also involved in making a record of crimes committed and of the perpetrators concerned when these people were members of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at the following page in the Croatian version, page 21; page 12 in the English version, and you have number 19 on the document. It's under the military police administration, and it says the following, I'll read out the second paragraph under the title "Military Police Administration": "Because of the increasingly complex situation in the territory of the HZ HB and the isolation of individual operative zones, it was planned to form light assault militaries police companies that would operate in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Assistant chiefs were appointed for the North-western Herzegovina operative zone, the Central Bosnia operative zone, and the Posavina operative zone. The powers of the military police administration chiefs were transferred to the UVP assistant chiefs, who were ordered to work as quickly as possible in organising light assault companies." Was this an attempt to try and link up the units in a more functional manner so that they were in a chain of command linking them up with the chief of particular operative zones? And this concerned the problems of communication that we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now have a look at the following page, 22 in the Croatian version, page 13 in the English version. I'll read out the paragraph. And you have the number 20 on the top of the page. "The military police administration's crime prevention department was transferred by transferring its powers to the operative zone level. This kind of organisation initially showed good results. Courses for officers dealing with problems of crime are being held at the training centre in Ljubuski. Employees of this department, in cooperation with employees of the internal affairs department, have been fully performing activities from within their own domain." When we read through this passage, would you agree with me if I said that this demonstrates that efforts were made to ensure that the crime department was professionally enabled and that they cooperated with the Ministry of the Interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at page 27 in the Croatian version. It's page 26 in the English version. And the number you have on the top is 25. It's the fourth paragraph in the English version, and the second paragraph in the Croatian version. Before I read that out, when you spoke to the investigators, you identified the problem of unauthorised entry into the prison, among other things, taking detainees out to perform labour. And when you assumed your duties, you were even informed of pressure exerted on military policemen who were hindered when it came to performing their duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll now read through this passage. "In the recent period in the area of the HB, over 6.000 prisoners of war were present in the centres. There are now over 4.000 detainees present." I'll now skip something. It says: "Significant number of detainees taken out to perform labour, which makes it possible for them to flee. There were a number of such cases, but we don't have the possibility of increasing the number of military policemen. The processing of detainees is being performed by SIS officials and the crime department officials. Wardens in prisons have been appointed and they're responsible for all tasks that include coordination. The military police have the task of providing security for the detainees. We have noticed that forcible entry has been made into these centres, and investigations or violent investigations have been carried out by certain commanders. This sort of behaviour must be forbidden and made impossible." You're familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as taking detainees out to perform labour, I wasn't aware of the fact that the military police provided security for all these centres, because according to the report of an acting officer dated the 22nd of November --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I didn't even think about that, but I think we agree that the military police did provide security, but I'm only asking you about the situation, where it provided security.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as taking them out to perform labour, that's correct. That was established later on. Violent investigations, I have no information about conducting investigations in a violent manner, but I have no reason to doubt that what is stated here is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to see page 29 in the Croatian version and page 17 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Seventeen? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, it's page 17 in the English version and it continues on page 18, the passage I will be reading out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll read out the second paragraph in the Croatian version and its penultimate paragraph in the English version. We're still dealing with the military police. "The chain of command was often broken because of the abuse of competence, and usurpation of powers." Tell me, were you familiar with this problem?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, there were problems within the system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at the following paragraph. It's on the same page in the Croatian version, and it continues in the English version. It says: "Over 3.000 military police organised in eight battalions form a compact military unit with a clearly defined position in the HVO structure. This is a wartime organisational structure which is sometimes inferior to the peacetime police structure, so that mistakes occur in the most ordinary police procedure. Light assault battalions participate in the most difficult war operations, achieving great successes, mostly with great sacrifices. Of 3.000 members of the military police, over 300 have been killed or seriously wounded." What I have read through confirms that during this period, too, the same problem was present, the problem that concerns the front line and the fact that the military police was engaged at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right up until mid-December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There is something else I'd like to have a brief look at in this document. It concerns the MUP during this period. It's page 35 in the Croatian version, page 21 in the Croatian version, and the number you have at the top is 31. Paragraph 6 in the English version -- or, rather, the first paragraph under the title the police department. It says: "The situation as far as law and order in the territory of the HZ H and B reflects the wartime situation throughout the territory. In such conditions, we believe that the situation of law and order is a particularly complex one, because the character of war is such that there are certain consequences. For example, theft and an increased level of all forms of crime." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at page 36 in the Croatian version and page 22 in the English version, paragraph two in both versions. "We should point out that over 50 per cent of these violations were committed by people in uniform." I'll skip the next part. It says: "According to the rules of service that are applicable, police officers intervened in cases involving uniformed persons, but such cases were immediately and without delay handed over to the military police." I think that this also demonstrates that at that period of time there was cooperation and coordination to the extent it was possible to have such cooperation and coordination between the military police and the civil police.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree would me if I said that one of the problems of the military police when dealing with crime was the fact that it wasn't quite clear what the authority of the civil police, the military police, and the SIS was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes. Who was responsible for what was not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we see P 00950 now. It's page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, before we move on to this document. General, when you assumed your duties in November did you have this type of document in your possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the sake of the transcript, I'd like to point out that on page 26 in the English version, it's page 563796, mention is made of war crimes, and it says that there were 256 persons who were concerned. There were 4 genocide -- cases of genocide, 31 war crimes against civilians, 149 cases of rebellion, 4 crimes committed against POWs, and 4 cases of destruction of companies, but it adds that all those concerned were Serbs. So I wanted to point that out. Counsel Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: While waiting for the document on the screen, the document I've referred to was P 00950, tell me, apart from the tasks of the military, police I have mentioned and the problems I have mentioned with regard to military police, is it correct to say that the military police had to carry out certain tasks that the civil police would usually carry out in peacetime? It was involved in the work of the border police in escorting humanitarian convoys. And when you assumed your duties you tried to alleviate the burden that the military police had in order to enable them to perform their duties with greater ease.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The document is -- represents the minutes from a session of the HZ HB. I think the date is the 28th of December, 1992, but it's not quite legible. But it is certainly December 1992. In the English version I'll be reading out page 3. It's page 2 in the Croatian version. It goes on to page 4, and it says: "Mr. Stojic mentions the problems caused by the fact that military courts were still not functioning, and he emphasised the fact that there were over 1.000 reports filed by the military police that hadn't been dealt with, and he also mentioned the problems of prisoners in the course of investigations. They cannot be detained without a court decision." I'll now step one passage and move on. "Mr. Stojic points out that our military police force cannot work without the military court, and they will release all the prisoners if military courts don't start functioning as soon as possible, and they will assume responsibility for this." Were you familiar with such a situation? As far as I can remember from your conversation with The Hague investigators, at the time that you arrived there the situation with the military courts and military prosecutor's office hadn't been solved. So you were trying to find people who were from Bosnia and Herzegovina but were in fact in Croatia, people who had the necessary professional expertise to start these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that the military police did file criminal reports, but that the military courts -- or, rather, the courts failed to react in a prompt manner, and we had these problems at the time I held my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 5D 00548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, very briefly. I don't want to intervene given our time restrictions, but this document notes that in December 1992 the military courts were practically not functioning because many cases hadn't been dealt with. You assumed your duties almost a year later, in November 1993, and we had the impression that at that time the situation had not advanced. Did you establish that the situation was the same or, rather, that the military courts weren't functions and that cases were still delayed, although that one year prior to this date attention had been drawn to this problem? Mr. Stojic himself had emphasised the existence of this problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand the question. I can't fully answer if because I wasn't responsible for the work of military prosecutors' offices and for military courts, but on the basis of what we discussed yesterday, I believed that there were certain shortcomings in the work of the prosecutor's office and the military courts. I also suggested to Mr. Susak that steps should be taken in this respect to help the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I wanted 5D 00548 on e-court, please. And it is a request for the re-investigation of the engagement of the military police units up at the front line of the 29th of September, 1993, request for re-examining of engagement of the units of the military police on the front lines. It was signed by the chief of the military police, Mr. Valentin Coric, and it says the following: "On a number of occasions we have warned and we're doing so again that the ministry -- military police administration, because of intensive and non-stop engage of the of the units of the military police on the front lines and at the same time due to the impossibility of bringing the units up to strength with new soldiers unable to perform the military police tasks according to its competence and authority. If the situation on the battlefield has been accepted and that the units of the military police in Central Bosnia and Posavina must be engaged up at the front lines, we are of the opinion that the total engagement of the military police in two zones in Herzegovina should be re-examined." I'd like to skip the next paragraph, and then later on we see the number of persons killed mentioned over the past five months. It says 11 kill, 74 severely wounded, 10 killed, 54 severely wounded, et cetera. I don't have time to read all the figures, but it says: "If this trend continues the military police will soon face a situation where it lacks the necessary number of men as is becoming a unit which is being extinguished, and crime is seriously on the increase and threatens to bring about anarchy on the hurt of the HZ HB. I announce with full responsibility that with the forces remaining after the schedule of the units of the military police on the front lines, we're not capable of performing regular military police tasks let alone more complex interventions and the more significant military political tasks. Because of the aforementioned, we demand that the engagement of the military police at the front lines be re-examined and we suggest that the military police forces be withdrawn from the front line so that they can carry out regular military police duties and that they should be sent to the front line only in exceptional circumstances." Do you agree with what it says here?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, from this can we see that Mr. Coric before you, before you took up your duties, endeavoured to save the military police from going to the front lines for the same reasons that you were able to apply later on when you took up your post?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, we have seen that this problem has -- has gone on and on. I have not forgotten your answer that in a moment of urgency it is necessary that the commanders take military police to engage in the front line, but that is understandable as an exception. The fact that here it seems to have been systematic. Does that not denote a fundamental defect in the organisation of the military activities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer, I'd like to complete the question or ask a complementary question, because this document is a very important one and testifies to the position of the author of this document, who is Mr. Coric. We have heard a whole series of witnesses testifying about the military actions that took place, and the modus operandi was briefly as follows. I haven't got a concrete case in mind, but in general terms the start of a military action. There was shelling first. After the shelling you have the military police. The military police arrests either combatants or civilians, to leave that for the moment, and then the people arrested by the military police, a number of witnesses have said that they were military police because they had their belts and so on. Anyway, the military police would take these people prisoner, arrest them. Then the proceedings are set in place and all the rest of it. So everything we have heard indicates that the military police was used in combat operations. Now, what I'd like to hear from you now is the following: Is it a basic task of the military police to be up at the front line and to take part in combat operations, because here we also see that -- we see the number of victims from amongst the ranks of the military police, and there were a great deal of casualties, fatalities and casualties in the military police which came about in action, in combat. So tell us, it was one of the tasks of the military police to be up at the front lines, and when you arrived in November, did you do anything to change the way in which the military police forces were deployed? So did you change things in such a way that after November the military police were no longer used in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the question and I'll try and answer as briefly as possible. It wasn't the basic being task of the military police to engage in combat operations, in offensive actions or defensive actions. When I arrived, I asked the chief of the General Staff, who was General Roso at the time, to issue an order for the withdrawal of the military police units from the front line. We were not able to achieve that in the month of November, but I think that sometime in mid-December we were successful in part and at the end of December all the military police forces were withdrawn from the front line. They remain longer at Rama -- or, rather, Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer, which was a very precise answer with respect to the withdrawal of troops -- or, rather, the military police forces as of November. That's what you told us, and that the decisions were taken in December and they were withdrawn from the front line, and we can see that on line 11 of page 75. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was a question posed by Judge Trechsel. I'm not sure whether Judge Trechsel is satisfied with -- it does cover in part but not in full, and I think it is a question that -- that deems worthy of being answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Indeed I think it was -- it was -- sort of got under an avalanche. Can you assess whether there was a fundamental organisational and planning defect which led to this habit of engaging military police for tasks which it is not equipped, trained, and -- and created for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm tempted to complement the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot assess the decisions of the commanders of the HVO and chief of the Main Staff of the day. I wish to believe that they were not along the lines of removing the military police from performing their military police tasks. I believe that they were guided by the need to defend Croatian lands. Of course, this had a negative effect on the work of the military police itself, and from my experience gained from the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, I led a military police unit in the Maslenica operation myself in 1993, so that this is not an exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for a very diplomatic answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, you wanted to say something in addition to what we have heard? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Witness, in Croatia the light assault battalions of the military police, were they precisely formed for that reason, to be able to take part in combat when the command deems necessary? Otherwise, it would appear that it was -- it depended on somebody's will. So is that correct, that they were formed to serve the defence of the territory and war, because why would the military police need to be in Zurich if Zurich were not taken over by some army? So it's defence first. It's not somebody's whim. It is the rules of combat that dictate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered this question yesterday -- or, rather, today, and let me state again. In the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, we had a light assault brigade, but it was established in order to perform combat assignments. I cannot claim why the light assault battalions of the military police were established, and with the new set-up and organisation they were abolished. I abolished them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. In the transcript I think that there is a mistake, whether in the transcript or the interpretation. It is line 76 [as interpreted]. I think the witness said that he cannot enter into the decisions of the Supreme Commander and Main Staff, where it says "commanders in the plural. So was it the Supreme Commander or commanders? Could the witness enlighten us? So who made the decision and why the decision was made and Judge Trechsel's answer was -- the witness said, "I cannot enter into the decisions of the main -- Supreme Commander."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the commander of the Croatian Defence Council and the chief of the Main Staff, because for a time there was the commander and after -- he was commander and afterwards he was chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. I heard you say "commander" in the singular, not commanders in the plural, because it says the plural in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow on from what Mr. Praljak said and the question I wanted to ask in addition, you're the first witness who seems to be best placed to speak about the military police. We have Mr. Coric, but as he's not testifying, you're the first witness who can give us a valid -- valid answers to the questions asked about the military police. Now, I have a question that I've been wanting to go ask you. We have had witnesses who have spoken to us about the fact that the military police were well equipped in terms of weapons, equipment and materiel, clothing, uniforms, et cetera. So one gained the impression that the military police was a highly disciplined unit, because in the army if you have discipline and discipline can be seen, it is in the military police. Now, by vocation, it is it up to you to address anybody who engages in infractions of military police law. So it's a well-disciplined unit. Now, one gains the impression that within those military police units there were individuals who were trained, as General Praljak -- along the lines that General Praljak said. So the high command, is that what motivated them to resort to these soldiers and use them on the grounds for offensive or defensive actions as you said? That's a hypothesis, a working hypothesis. But as you are a specialist in the area and this is the first time that we actually have a specialist here to answer our questions, and you're an a high-ranking officer, it would be interesting to hear your views on that. That's why I'm asking you the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the military police units in general terms should really be the best equipped part of the armed forces in applying their authority within the military police remit. Of course, members of the military police are trained in other skills, too, but the military police units don't have the equipment necessary. Well, I don't know what the light assault brigades had -- battalions had, but usually they are not commensurate to combat activities, and they usually just have light weapons. But let me stress again that it is standard practice in the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia during the homeland war that when the situation demanded it, of course for a short period of time, we, too, as members of the military police, the armed forces of Croatia, were engaged in combat assignments. But not for long periods, and not in large numbers as it says in the report by the chief, Mr. Valentin Coric, dated the 29th of December. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock. Can we take a break so that I could summarise and look through the questions that I still want to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That will give the registrar some time to do the maths. We reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Tomic, you have 26 minutes left. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at document P 00957. Could we have that document on the screen. It concerns the structure of the HVO military police, dated the 26th of December, 1992. To make it easier for everyone to follow, I'll start with the second paragraph, and I'll read out the first sentence of every paragraph, and then I'll read the last two paragraphs on the last page. Since that will be sufficient for my purposes. It says: "The 1st Battalion of the military police is active and it's directly tied to the military police administration and its chief and it is active in the entire territory of the HZ HB. The 2nd Battalion has its headquarters in Tomislavgrad and covers the North-western Herzegovina operative zone. The 3rd Battalion has its headquarters in Mostar and covers operative zone of eastern Herzegovina. The 4th Battalion has its headquarters in Travnik, Vitez, and covers the operative zone of Central Bosnia. The 5th Battalion is for the Posavina operative zone." And the last two paragraphs: "The battalion commanders and military police commanders in operative zones, when carrying out their daily tasks shall be immediately subordinated to the commander of the operative zone. They shall carry out all orders that concern military police duties and are in accordance with authorities and responsibilities of the military police. Military police platoons in brigades shall carry out orders of the brigade commander and shall do so within the field of responsibility." Tell me, are you familiar with this structure?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is this structure clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to have a look at 5D 00538. These are the minutes that concern coordination with commanders of the operative zone of north-Western Herzegovina. It's dated the 9th of March, 1993. It's been signed by commander Zeljko Siljeg. Item 1 shows that the subject was the structure and the tasks of the military police. And on the following page we have the first item. This is what I will now read out. Item 1, I will read out two paragraphs. You'll see what is concern. "The commander of the operative zone presented the main problems that related to establishing and commanding and controlling the military police. According to the establishment scheme, establishment scheme for structuring this force, the 2nd Battalion of the military police in this operative zone -- is in this operative zone and under its command. And equipping, training -- and equipping and training shall be carried out by the military police administration. Brigades in their zones of responsibility can use units of military police that have been formed in their zones of responsibility. Military police platoons and brigades shall be formed by all brigades that shall equip them, train them, and they are exclusively the responsibility of the brigades and in accordance with the line -- and this shall be done in accordance with the line of command, with the chain of command. The commander of the military police when carrying out military police tasks is immediately subordinated to the commander of the operative zone, and military police platoons within brigades shall carry out orders of the brigade commander and shall do so within the field of their responsibility. When engaging the military police, the commander of the military zone shall inform the chief of the military police administration, and when the military police is engaged by the brigade commander he shall inform the commander of the operative zone, and the commander of the military police battalion." And now let's have a look at the following page, the last paragraph, page 3 in the English version, third paragraph on the same page in the Croatian version, it says: "The military police in the OZCH when so ordered shall provide daily regular and interim reports to the operative zone and to the brigades. The commander of the operative zone shall authorise the chief of the SIS of the operative zone North-western Herzegovina to command the military police battalion." As far as I have understood from your testimony to date, one of the main problems that concerns the military police was that often the role of the military police was misunderstood in the field, and the way in which orders were issued and the way in which the chain of command functioned was misunderstood. So such coordination is the result of such problems. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we now have document P 01678 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just pick up on this? We have seen now that in the practical operation the military police is under the command of the commander of the operational zone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what has been read out here, yes, what concerns carrying out military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And the commander of the operation zone in turn is in line of command under the chief of staff. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So then one can say that there is a line of command from the chief of staff to the military police as far as the operational work is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to daily operative orders, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would also like to ask a question concerning this document which was now introduced by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. That is the document 00538. And in this document you will find -- there is no page numbers here but only the number of 2749, 2749, and this part starts with the following: "Briefing by commanders in areas of responsibility." And the first -- the first paragraph speaks about the Petar Kresimir for the 4th Brigade presented by Martin Kulis, deputy commander. I wonder if the interpreters found it, but I hope that's yes. And in that very briefing there is an interesting sentence. It says that they, meaning I believe the Petar Kresimir Brigade, "They have joined up their left wing with the HV Croatian army forces in the Peruca." So I repeat the sentence. They have joined up the HV Croatian army forces in the Peruca direction." I would like to ask the witness -- of course I do not know the region and I do not know if the Peruca direction, it was still within Herceg-Bosna or was it in the Republic of Croatia, and the joining the left wing meant a kind of military operation and military cooperation, or it was at the borderline where they have actually joined up their wings. So it is my question to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand your question. Peruca is in the Republic of Croatia. However, it's very close to the border between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Croatian army forces, I assume these were units from Sinj. I'm referring to the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. They held the line there, and they reach the border. I believe the Petar Kresimir Brigade came from the border on the other side. And contact was established in the sense that there was no no man's area. So the HVO forces were in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of the Croatian army in Croatia. That's how I understand this part here. There was no empty space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Could we have P 01678 on the screen. First the first page. In the English version it's on the second page, 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a response with regard to the conclusions from the minutes. It's been signed by Valentin Coric. In the first paragraph it says the following: "The -- this -- in the document on the structure of the military police, it states that when carrying out daily police tasks the commander of the battalion, the 2nd Battalion of the OZ should be immediately under the commander of the operative zone, and the commanders of operative platoons immediately under the brigade commander. The military police shall also carry out individual requests or commands from the chief of the SIS, but the chief of the SIS of the operative zone cannot receive general authorisation to command the military police battalion as this is in violation of the regulations on organisation of the defence department and regulations on the organisation of the military police administration. The operative zone commander is not competent to change these regulations by his decision or command. "Therefore, the operative zone commander shall be responsible, and if he is absent an individual officer shall replace him. Responsibility cannot be transferred to the chief of the SIS in general terms." Would you agree with me that this document is an attempt by Mr. Coric to establish the structure to those to whom it's not clear and to avoid future misunderstandings when it comes to the military police and its responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we now have the following document: P 04262. This is a warning from Mr. Petkovic on behalf of the Main Staff of the HVO, dated the 17th of August, 1993. The title is "The brigade military police responsibilities -- or, rather, command responsibilities," and it says: "Quite frequently the inefficiency of the brigade military police is a subject of which the commanders often contact the chief of the military police. I here by warn the brigade military police is under the direct command of brigade commanders. It is also within the brigades and has the status as another unit of the brigade. Recruiting manpower is to be carried out only from the military structure of a brigade, and the commander has the right to replace every military policeman. The chief of the military police can only be asked for professional assistance. All problems within the brigade police are your problems, and you should solve them through the system of command." As far as I know, you have also encountered problems with the brigade police.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the system of command was not clear -- or, rather, they were outside the system, and for this reason this was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to move on to another area now. When we talked over of the past few days, we discussed a question, according to the information you received and as was explained to you, there were just two military prisons in the period before you arrived and when you arrived. There were Ljubuski and Heliodrom; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about a report of the acting head of the military police who informed me that under the authority of the military police Ljubuski and Heliodrom were under them, and Gabela were under the Home Guard Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecutor showed you a document. I'm not going to look for the number now, but I'll remind you of it, it was a document for the record P 07494, which Mr. Pusic -- a document which Mr. Pusic addressed to you asking that people be transferred from Heliodrom to Gabela, and in your own handwriting you wrote that you did not agree with that. You remember the document that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When I read the transcript from your interview with the investigators from The Hague, when you were shown this document and you were asked for your explanation why you wrote that you didn't agree, among other things you said that because you considered that it says that Gabela was the military police investigation prison, whereas you didn't consider it to be a military investigating prison. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that point in time Gabela was no longer topical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the information that you had before that you received from Mr. Lavric to the effect that Gabela -- that Gabela was under the home guard security system.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when we were discussing prisons earlier on, you said that when your arrival you instructed people to comply with the Geneva Conventions and conduct with the POWs but that you did not know whether anybody did this before you.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not look to see whether this was stated before, but I wrote the instructions and manual again because you can never have too much of a good thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, there was another document, document P 06805. You don't have to look for the document, I'll just remind you. They were answers by Mr. Lavric to your questions. I think you had some 10 questions, or 13 questions that you asked him, and he responded to those questions, and we can check this out later on, but within the frameworks of those questions he relates to the instructions and order given by Mr. Coric linked to Heliodrom of the 22nd of September, 1992. I don't know whether you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we have on e-court the following document P 00514, which is instructions on the work of the central military prison of the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar dated the 22nd of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have the number again?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And it is signed by the head, Valentin Coric, and under item 1 it says: "The duties of the commander of the central prison," and among other things under point 2 it says that he is responsible for ensuring that prisoners of war are treated in conformity with the 1949 Geneva Conventions. Then similarly on page 8 of the English version, page 8, please, and in the Croatian version it is on page 4, and it says: "Home rules in the central military prison of the HVO in Mostar," and it says what prisoners of war are, what military prisoners are. Under point 3 it says that all POWs should be treated in compliance with the 1949 Geneva Conventions. Under point 4 it stipulates the right of prisoners to medical assistance, health care, and so on. Would you agree that this in a sense are also a sense of instructions as to how to -- prisoners of war are to be treated, the same kind of instructions that you gave previously?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are guidelines an instructions which refer to everyone, not only to the central military prison. This is more detailed and prescribes how the work should be done in practice. I should like to say that when I first met Mr. Valentin Coric and when our two administrations cooperated in 1992 we personally handed to him our set of our instructions which we applied in Croatia, so that already at that time he was interested in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we now have on e-court the following document P 03651. It is a document from the crime prevention department of the military police describing the decisions reached at a meeting held in Ljubuski on the 22nd of July, 1993, in the military police administration, signed by Mr. Vidovic, and I'm going to read the portions that are of interest to me, paragraphs 2, 3, and 4. At the meeting it was reiterated what the activities and competence of the crime prevention department were. It was assessed that direct cooperation with the active police force, that is the military police and MUP and the district military court, was good and the decision was wholly clear and there was no overlap, while our cooperation with officers of the central military remand prison must be indirect, and this is realised through the institution of the District Military Court for which we process crimes to the extent of evaluating whether there are grounds for bringing criminal proceedings to bear and the SIS inasmuch as cooperation is necessary. Thus all detained persons without -- where criminal proceedings had not been taken or a criminal report filed are on the -- according to the order of the chief of the military police administration unknown to our department. This refers solely to a large number of Muslims who were brought indiscriminately to the SVIZ prison and after that they were forgotten. Through inertia the crime prevention department conducted interviews with over 2.000 people but not a single one of them was of any interest as far as crime was concerned. The question posed by Mr. Coric, chief of the military police administration, regarding our duties was therefore justified and was the reason for them issuing the above order for us to start dealing with crime. "After the head of the department of administration and justice had had to produce a report on the SVIZ pursuant to the decision of this department, it was the task of the warden of the SVIZ, as well as adopting all decisions regarding detainees." There seems to be an error in the transcript. Just a moment I'll read it again. "Since the head of the department of administration and justice was duty-bound to compile an a report on SVIZ pursuant to the decisions of the institutions of this department, it was the task of the department of justice to appoint the warden of the SVIZ as well as adopting all decisions regarding detainees." Tell me, please, in this document are the duties of the military police properly defined as well as the role of the military court with respect to the prisons and the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Everything is clear. You say -- I would like to know what the sentence -- the following sentence means: "As concern disciplinary measures as against HVO soldiers, these will be decided by the person issuing them." It seems a bit redundant, that the decision is decided by the person issuing the decision. Maybe it's a problem of translation. MS.
