TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I think that that's what it says, exactly as you read it, and what it means is this, I think: It is the disciplinary code of conduct or rules which I haven't time to go into but which we went into with Mr. Tomljanovich, and the witness said something about that yesterday, but I can advise you to look at the following document, which is document -- well, Judge Trechsel, you can check it out there, P 00293, Article 19 and 29. I think that it will be clearer, because this sentence is indeed rather confusing. So it's -- P 00293, Articles 19 and 29 will provide a fuller explanation of what that sentence means, and I'd like now to move on to the next document, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want to say it makes common sense to tell me to look it up, but it's not actually adversarial procedures. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but it's very difficult for me to comment on what this actually means. Mr. Coric is going to throw light onto the matter. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I am going to ask the General a question. If any HVO commander were to issue a disciplinary measure, for instance, 15 days in prison for violation of offences, 15 days in detention, then that detention would be served at Heliodrom. So that, Mr. -- Judge Trechsel, is what this refers to. Is that right, Witness? Is that an answer to what the Judge asked in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, yes, I'm clear on what this means. It is disciplinary measures which come under the competence of the commander of the HVO in a given circumstance, and I think that when I arrived we freed the military police of detaining people who were in detention through a disciplinary measure that has been taken, and that is the case in armies all over the world. So the sentence, as far as I'm concerned, is clear. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Can -- Your Honours, may I ask the witness one more question? Do you know that when Heliodrom was established, that is to say in September, it was a facility where such sentences were served as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know there were members of the HVO there who were serving disciplinary sentences. I don't know which documents justified this, but I have no reason to doubt that this was the case. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It took more time than I anticipated and it leaves things less clear than they were before for me but I shall not insist. Sorry for taking -- interrupting you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we now see document P 04756 on the screen. These are the minutes from a session of the heads of defence -- the defence department held on the 2nd of December, 1993. Could we see the document on the screen, Croatian version page 3, and the English version page 4. I'll read out three brief paragraphs. "Then Mr. Coric presented certain problems that the military police encounters. Above all, given engagement of the military police at the front line, the quality of the military police's composition has been adversely affected. Materiel is being taken away from the command of various individuals. There's the brigade police that's not part of the military police. And similarly the work in military prisons is very poor. The head wanted to take the floor and said the following: 'I believe that we have two military prisons, the Heliodrom and the military prison in Ljubuski. As for other places where detainees are being held, in Gabela and Dretelj, I don't consider them to be military facilities,' and refused to personally endorse the work of these institutions." Tell me, does this reflect everything that you knew about when you arrived there? This isn't new information.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to interpret something and said that Heliodrom and Ljubuski were under the military police. According to a report of the officer responsible, the home Guards Unit were providing security for Gabela. I don't know whether this responsibility was such, Ministry of Defence later on, I didn't establish this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say under the military police or, rather, the responsibility of the military police, does this mean that the military police provided security?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the Heliodrom and in Ljubuski, according to the report of the chief, acting chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On a number of occasions you have told me that when you arrived at the site -- and later on you did not find out who was responsible for the detention units or the prisons. It doesn't matter what we call them.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at the last document that I will showing you, P 06848. I'll read out the last paragraph. This is a report from the SVIZ warden. Josip Praljak has signed the document. It's dated the 24th of November, 1993. The report was addressed to General Roso, Mr. Lavric, and Mr. Jukic. The report states the following: "I believe that it is high time to take steps to ensure that the prison functions more adequately and to provide better security, and to decide who can issue orders on allowing detainees to be taken out to perform labour, and to see who is responsible for the SVIZ in Mostar." Tell me, is this a good reflection of the events, of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't seen this report. I hope that the person who sent it provided a correct description of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have another question. When my colleague, Ms. Alaburic, cross-examined you, she asked you about detainees being taken out to perform labour and about who had the authority to send people out to perform labour. You were asked whether the warden could refuse to give -- or to hand over detainees, to help them if they had a legitimate request. You said that in practice things worked in a somewhat different manner, but you didn't really explain this. Can you tell me what the situation was when it came to practice? Could Mr. Bozic, the warden, have said that when he received request or an order or an approval, I don't care what we call this document at this point in time, but when he received such a document how would he act?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in legal terms, officially, yes, he could act in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But could he have in practice refused to comply with such an order? What would be the consequences have been?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in practice I never saw such a case. He didn't refuse such permission if he had been provided with such a request. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more questions. Perhaps there is some time left for Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would appear that the 75 minutes have been used up. Mr. Coric, your time has been used up unless Mr. Ibrisimovic will give you a few minutes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already told Mr. Karnavas that I would let him have some of my time, so I have no additional time. I'll use the time left until the end of this session. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I have no time to put questions to the witness, would you at least allow me to say that -- or would you at least allow me to inform you of the subjects I wanted to touch on, if possible? If not, well, that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think in light of the time that we have left, that is we have all day tomorrow, plus we have some time today, I don't see allowing Mr. Coric 10 or 15 minutes would effect us finishing this witness on time, in light of what I have and what the Stojic team has. So I think this is one exception, especially since Mr. Coric was the head of the military police, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but one exception after another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's the first exception I've asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Mundis, what is it that you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to put on the record that we have 10 or 15 minutes of redirect, if that's possible, for tomorrow but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may remind you that I haven't used up all of my time, so perhaps I could retroactively give the Coric Defence that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You have. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have given Mr. Prlic your 60 minutes. That's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's a slight misunderstanding. I gave Mr. Prlic the time I wasn't going to use; those to Mr. Coric, the matter is in your hands. It's not for me to decide who will use up the time allocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, you have 10 minutes. Please go ahead, but you should have reached an agreement with your counsel when it comes to the questions that you wanted to ask. Please go ahead, you have 10 minutes. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I'd like to thank everyone who has made this possible. Cross-examination by the Accused Coric:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, yesterday you said that we would meet and see each other during the wartime period. Could you briefly describe our cooperation at the time? Were we partners from two states? Did we have such a relationship on a permanent basis or was one person superior to another? Could you say something very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Coric, for that question. From the very beginning of the combat in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, from the very beginning we had the relationship that exists between partners, and we mutually respected each other. That's my experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My following question, General, concerns the prisons. Are you aware of the fact that in Herceg-Bosna we had prisoners before we had prisons?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that neither that, not on the basis of any documents but I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Herceg-Bosna there was no hospital for the mentally ill throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never really gave much thought to the matter, but there's no reason for me not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm putting this question to you because I know that we have to respect the fact that such ill people were in the streets, and I'm talking about the general security situation. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On a number of occasions my counsel mentioned the problem of responsibility for prisons. Are you aware of the fact that some prisons were established at local levels?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Some prisons were secured by Ministry of the Interior staff?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Others by the home guard and others by the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as in the case of Rama, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We could discuss that matter in detail. What I would now like to ask you is, would it be logical for someone to suggest that a central military prison be established very rapidly? In April the conflict started, and this suggestion was made in June.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did one react rapidly and was a prison established on the 22nd of September? Was that fast, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's from June to September, I wouldn't say that that is fast, if I have understood your question correctly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, that might be the case too. As for the central military prison, which did not exist at all, was it time to take the decision, to construct the facility, to find the staff?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak mentions money.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the first staff team at the Heliodrom after the 22nd of September was mostly composed of security officers from the former district prison in Mostar? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during that period of time even the prisoners in the district prison had been placed at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I subsequently found out about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You saw the establishment and organisation and the instructions given to the warden that was appointed on the 22nd of September. Do you know that the head of the military police administration until the end of his term of office, that is to say October or November of 1993 - that was me - that apart from that signature on that document there were no direct written or oral instructions to the prison warden?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but I'm not aware of any document which would say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to the military police work. I think the two of us should know what it entails. Now, in the prison itself, if we're speaking about the central military prison at Heliodrom, you need to provide security for the detainees. Now, from everything that you saw, was that job done by the Military Police Platoon within the 5th Battalion of the military police in Mostar? Did they provide that service?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And does that come under the work of the military police, to secure the detainees? Did the police do its work?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in peacetime. In wartime the military police does provide security for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the crime investigation department, that's another area that the military police does, and you had a report from Mr. Vidovic of Mostar. Is that something that the military police also engages in?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the third thing that the military police does in a prison, and I'm referring to the Heliodrom now, is to transfer detainees and to ensure security for them from one prison to another, and let me tie this up, to provide security and escorts when there are exchanges or when detainees are taken to hospital, for example. Does that come under the remit of the military police as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, did you ever see any other work done by the military police at my time in relation to the detainees? Do you have a document that comes to mind perhaps about some other assignments?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When in Ljubuski at a meeting with the heads of departments I expounded on the work of the crime prevention military police and their work with detainees in that regard, then in his report Mr. Vidovic says that I instructed that cooperation with the warden be indirect. Does that bring to mind all the things that I said, that there is no command and orders issued towards the warden?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there's another unwieldy construction there in Mr. Vidovic's writings, but how did you understand him when he said that after my explanation that the crime prevention police can only talk to people and decide about their fate if they are being criminally investigated, when Vidovic said that everybody else as far as the military police are concerned are unknown? Does that come within the general concept of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood this part of what Mr. Vidovic said correctly, then I consider that he was speaking about individuals who had committed certain offences and crimes and that these are the people that the crime investigation police were interested in, not the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And now my last question and last topic are the light assault soldiers. Now, would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Light assault forces. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- that the light assault forces and units were established first and foremost as units for anti-terrorist combat? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that in Croatia they were exclusively intended for combat operations, and so I assume that what you say is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The light assault units were units which intervened, went into action, if the regular forces who held the front line lost their positions at the front line. Then somebody had had to intervene quickly with light weapons. You know the kind of light weapons that the light assault forces had. Is that part of their job too?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that that could be part of their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When defensive operations or offensive operation are being carried out, does the military police provide security for the zone of combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should do, yes. An entry and exit from the zone of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, usually, generally speaking, such operations within the frameworks of the military police, are they accompanied and followed by smaller units of light assault forces who intervene if the defence positions are being lost? Is that, too, the job of the light assault forces?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can be deployed in that manner as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: However, were you witness to the fact that there were abuses of military police units, that some commanders who held command over certain parts of the front line and certain positions used the light assault forces for days and months to guard the line? Were you witness of that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the situation I came across when I arrived. I found light assault forces up at the line and now -- the military policemen also up at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that after my departure from the military police, that is to say at the beginning of the November when you arrived, that I left 162 killed military fighters behind me and over 500 wounded do you know about that figure, those figures?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and I think there may have been more people killed than the figure you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the period when I was there. And finally, we cooperated at a time when I was minister of the interior. Do you remember that by coordinating our work and engaging in joint activities we performed the following activities: First the MUP took over the border. MUP took over the escort -- provided escorts for humanitarian conveys and that we withdrew both police forces from the front line and that we formed a joint sabotage units -- intervention forces, rather, in all the municipalities, and that we solved the motion difficult problems together jointly? Would you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to all those questions is in the affirmative. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you have any complaints with respect to my work or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have overstepped the time. You took 15 minutes, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, I'll give him a couple of minutes, I think. But I must say and I must complain that this is the sort of questioning that we should be getting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How does this concern you? It is Mr. Coric's problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Overall. Overall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a general rule, we can stay here for hours, but we have been extremely flexible in giving Mr. Coric 15 minutes, whereas his counsel had 75 minutes, and he's not complaining, Mr. Coric isn't complaining, you're complaining, unless you're going to take over the defence of Mr. Coric. If so, tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am making an observation on behalf of all of the accused because this seems to be a constant topic among us. And, Your Honour, you indicated that for the first time we have an expert and now we have two experts and I think this is to help you. And I'm not defending Mr. Coric, but I'm defending every -- my own client because I want to be treated the same way. So I think a couple of minutes is not going to kill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have two hours. You will have two hours for addressing all the issues. Mr. Coric, since you are the principal person concerned, what do you wish to add? THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Well, I would end with this question. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas; I would have a lot of questions to ask Mr. Biskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, my last question was can you tell Their Honours, can you tell the Judges whether you ever complained about our cooperation during both periods when I was head of the military police administration and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I've already answered that question. I never had any problems, nor did I consider that you in any way obstructed anything or in any way attempted to obstruct my work after your departure from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, in answer to a question of Mr. Coric, you have said that there were no command and orders issued towards the warden. I am not quite sure what -- what this means. Were you saying that the chief of the military police had no authority over the warden of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't say that. The question that Mr. Coric asked me was whether I had seen, apart from the home rule -- house rules, whether I saw any special orders or separate orders or anything else, and I said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a question I'm going to ask you, which concerns you and has less to do with the accused, but it's a question which follows on from what Mr. Praljak was demonstrating -- demonstrating yesterday with regard to dual citizenship. If I understood you correctly, you said you arrived in the month of November because you thought that having been important in Bosnia-Herzegovina it was your duty to be present, to be there with your compatriots who were in the same situation as you were. So it was under those conditions that you joined the ranks of the HV. Do you agree with what I've said so far, the summary I've made of your position so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree. However, it says "the Croatian army." It should say HVO. Not HV but HVO. The ranks of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, several months ago we had the American ambassador who was in Zagreb, and he met Mr. Tudjman, and the witness who testified said that the American government let Mr. Tudjman understand that there were important changes at the level of the HVO, and the witness told us that there were two individuals who were concerned, Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Praljak. And the ambassador who was a witness told us that they -- these people were removed after that. Now, if we look at this chronologically, how the events came to pass, it is important to note that this happened in November, that is to say the precise time when you arrived there to take up your duties. And on the basis of the documents that we looked through here, we saw that you did an enormous task because you made decisions every day, wrote reports every day, and that you did a great amount of work. But what I'm interested in is whether your arrival over there in the month of November was the result of your personal initiative or did somebody at the level of Croatia, the Croatian government, did someone from the Croatian government ask you whether you could go over there and try and assist in military organisation or organisation in general terms? So did you do so at your own initiative, because you decided to, or did somebody instruct you to do so and ask you to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether I said this yesterday or the day before, but when I talked to the Prosecutors, at the beginning of the war on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina I asked to go to Posavina, which is where my extended family lived, my family and my wife's family. However, because of the duties in the ministry of the defence of the Republic of Croatia, I was not able to engage directly in the HVO, and until I went to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna I always had this wish, this desire, and the people whom I worked with knew about that, knew about this wish of mine. And I have already explained how I came to go to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and if need be I'll repeat those reasons. So I did not go there pursuant to an order of any kind. I considered what Mr. Bobetko -- General Bobetko said, but it was simply a way of fulfilling our duties the way each of us felt, that they should go to help the country they were born in and the people they belonged to. I don't know how you linked up the departure of Mr. Praljak and the late Mr. Mate Boban. I don't know how they left. I know that General Praljak left before we arrived. As to Mr. Boban, I think he was still there when I left the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. He remained as president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that very clear answer. It is 7.00. The Prlic Defence will have two hours, 60 minutes, plus 60 minutes given by Mr. Pusic, which makes two hours. And as far as Mr. Stojic is concerned, 75 minutes. Is that right, Counsel Ibrisimovic, because I have the impression that there have been calculation problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we're trying to establish a scheduling order. I didn't say that I gave all my time to Mr. Prlic, but the time left over from my cross-examination of this witness, any time left over. I won't use all my time. I'll just deal with what the witness did when he arrived vis-a-vis Mr. Pusic and what he did. I won't deal with the other accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, you're going to start off your cross-examination tomorrow, and if there's any time left over from your 60 minutes you're going to give that time to Mr. Prlic. So that is -- seems to be very precise. And I think Mr. Karnavas will have two hours or -- well, anyway, it's 7.00. I invite you back for our sitting at 2.15.
